strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: controllable concept erasure in diffusion models with interpretable interventions rather than full model fine-tuning. The proposed supervised SAE idea is simple, plausible, and well motivated by the feature-splitting problem in unsupervised SAEs.

The main empirical results are promising. On UnlearnCanvas object unlearning, SAEMNESIA improves the reported average metric from 82.29 for SAeUron to 91.51, with gains in UA, IRA, and CRA. The sequential unlearning experiment is also compelling, with much better 9-object UA and retention than the SAE baseline.

The paper includes several useful analyses beyond a single benchmark table: score histograms, top-1-latent k-NN evidence, qualitative patch visualizations, multiplier sweeps, ablations over supervised variants, standard deviations over 4 seeds, adversarial-prefix experiments, and I2P nudity-removal results.

The method has a practical efficiency advantage at inference: if the concept-to-latent mapping is reliable, searching only multiplier values instead of latent subsets is a meaningful simplification, and the paper quantifies this clearly.
Presentation is mostly readable and the paper does a good job connecting mechanistic interpretability concepts to diffusion model unlearning.
weaknesses: The central one-concept/one-latent claim is not fully established. The supervised loss encourages assigned latents to activate for present concepts, but the paper provides limited evidence that the concept is not still represented elsewhere, especially beyond selected UnlearnCanvas concepts. The nudity experiment itself weakens the one-latent story: the one-latent version is worse than SAeUron, and the best result requires steering two latents with a very large multiplier.

The evaluation scope is narrow relative to the claims. Most results are on SD v1.x and UnlearnCanvas with structured object/style prompts and one selected UNet block. The method may depend strongly on clean prompt-derived labels, predefined concepts, and benchmark-specific concept structure; generalization to open-vocabulary, compositional, copyrighted, or more ambiguous concepts is not demonstrated.

Comparison fairness and reproducibility need more detail. The paper says it found an inconsistency in SAeUron's public metric computation and recomputed metrics, but does not explain the bug or provide enough detail to independently verify the corrected comparison. Key implementation details such as SAE dimensionality, TopK value, training schedule, data volume after activation extraction, compute cost, exact prompt lists/splits, and code release are insufficiently specified in the main text.

The claimed 96.67% hyperparameter-search reduction is somewhat overstated because it counts only inference-time latent subset search and ignores the added supervised training, label construction, validation scoring, and per-concept multiplier tuning. The appendix also shows sensitivity to beta and multiplier choices, including complete white images for beta=10, suggesting the method is not as plug-and-play as implied.

The safety and ethics treatment is thin. The paper evaluates nudity suppression and adversarial prompts, but does not discuss dual-use risks of controllable concept manipulation, detector bias/failure modes in NudeNet, possible over-erasure of benign content, or the implications of training on COCO captions for NSFW removal.

There are presentation and notation issues that reduce clarity: duplicated explanatory sentences in the results section, overloaded gamma notation for both decorrelation weighting and unlearning multipliers, awkward or incomplete equation formatting, and limited explanation of some appendix variants. These are fixable but matter for reproducibility.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem: interpretable and efficient concept erasure in diffusion models, where SAE feature splitting is a real obstacle for controllable interventions.

The central idea of using prompt-derived supervision to encourage stronger concept-latent associations is plausible and useful. The method is simple, and the claimed reduction in latent-combination search is a meaningful practical advantage if the one-to-one mappings hold.

The evaluation covers several relevant axes beyond a single benchmark, including UnlearnCanvas retention/erasure metrics, sequential unlearning, multiplier sensitivity, adversarial prompts, nudity suppression, and qualitative visualizations.
The appendix reports ablations over several SAE variants, standard deviations for the main method, multiplier comparisons, and failure cases such as weaker nudity centralization with one latent.
weaknesses: The central claim of one-to-one concept-neuron mapping is not fully supported. The training labels are prompt-level labels assigned to all spatial activations and timesteps, which is a noisy supervision signal for localized visual concepts. The proposed CA loss only encourages assigned latents to activate on positive samples; it does not directly penalize activation on negative samples or prove that other latents stop encoding the concept. L1 sparsity and decorrelation are an indirect proxy, not a convincing guarantee of feature centralization.

The evaluation is too narrow for the strength of the claims. Most results are on SD v1.x and UnlearnCanvas object categories, with only one U-Net block emphasized. The paper calls the method architecture agnostic but does not test other diffusion architectures, other layers, or stronger contemporary erasure benchmarks beyond a limited I2P experiment.

Comparisons are not sufficiently rigorous. The authors state that they found an inconsistency in SAeUron's public implementation and recomputed metrics, but the corrected protocol is not described in enough detail to audit. Several recent baselines cited in related work are not included in the main UnlearnCanvas comparison. It is also unclear whether all methods receive comparable hyperparameter tuning budgets, which matters because the paper's efficiency claim is partly about search cost.

Some results undercut the strongest narrative. Nudity removal requires steering two latents, not one, and the single-latent SAEMNESIA result is worse than SAeUron. Sequential unlearning uses a hand-selected subset of nine objects rather than the full benchmark or multiple orderings, so the scalability claim remains preliminary.

The adversarial robustness evidence is weakly presented. SAEMNESIA still drops from 73.30% to 28.30% unlearning accuracy after attack, which is a large degradation. The paper frames this as strong robustness mainly relative to a weak attacked baseline, without sufficient analysis of attack transfer, stronger attacks, or whether the remaining performance is practically safe.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The manuscript gives high-level data construction and some hyperparameters, but important details are missing or scattered: exact SAE size and expansion, training compute, optimizer settings, batch sizes, selected timesteps/layers, validation split, classifier details, prompt sets, and code availability are not clearly specified.

Presentation has several issues that reduce confidence: repeated sentences, notation inconsistencies around gamma as both decorrelation weight and inference multiplier, unclear normalization in Eq. 10, and overstrong language such as establishing a new standard despite limited scope. The limitations and ethics discussion is minimal for a paper about suppressing unsafe or copyrighted content.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and useful idea: adding prompt-derived supervision to SAE training so diffusion-model concepts are concentrated into designated latents, enabling more targeted inference-time erasure. This is a meaningful extension over unsupervised SAE-based unlearning and is well motivated by the feature-splitting problem.

The empirical results on UnlearnCanvas are strong: SAEMNESIA improves the reported average score over SAeUron from 82.29% to 91.51%, with gains in UA, IRA, and CRA, and includes standard deviations over four seeds for the main result.

The paper evaluates beyond the headline benchmark, including sequential object unlearning, uniform multiplier sweeps, adversarial prefix attacks, qualitative visualizations, concept-interference analyses, and I2P nudity suppression. These extra studies make the contribution more convincing than a single benchmark table would.

The method has practical appeal because it avoids modifying the base diffusion model weights and reduces the latent-combination search needed by prior SAE methods. The computational-efficiency argument is simple and compelling when the one-concept/one-latent assumption holds.

Presentation is generally clear, with helpful figures illustrating the pipeline, concept-score concentration, qualitative removals, and sequential unlearning behavior. The appendix contains useful ablations over loss variants and reports cases where some configurations fail or underperform.
weaknesses: The central claim of one-to-one concept-latent mapping is not fully established. The CA loss encourages assigned latents to activate for positive samples, but the evidence for exclusive localization is mostly score histograms for a few concepts and K-NN plots without detailed quantitative tables. Some appendix results still show substantial concept interference and difficult cases such as flames and jellyfish.

The scope of the supervision is narrower than some claims suggest. Labels are cheap only when concepts are explicitly present in templated prompts, and the method is evaluated mainly on object/style concepts from UnlearnCanvas. It is less clear how well it scales to open-vocabulary, compositional, ambiguous, or naturally captioned concepts where prompt-derived labels are noisy or incomplete.

The comparison around hyperparameter-search reduction is somewhat idealized. SAEMNESIA still requires multiplier selection, and the best main benchmark appears to use per-concept searched multipliers. The 96.67% reduction is plausible relative to SAeUron's latent-combination search, but does not fully account for supervised SAE training cost, concept assignment, or validation needed for new concept sets.

The nudity-removal result is promising but weakens the paper's single-latent narrative: the one-latent SAEMNESIA variant underperforms SAeUron substantially on I2P, and the best result uses TOP2 with a very large multiplier. This is honestly disclosed, but it shows that centralization may fail for imbalanced or broad safety concepts.

Evaluation depends heavily on classifier-based metrics and benchmark classifiers. The paper would be stronger with more direct human or VLM-based assessment of whether concepts are truly removed while visual quality and prompt fidelity are preserved, especially because unlearning can exploit classifier blind spots.

Reproducibility is adequate but not complete from the manuscript alone. The appendix gives several hyperparameters and ablations, but implementation details such as training duration, dataset splits, exact activation extraction/storage, compute budget, code availability, and full baseline rerun protocol are not specified in enough detail to make independent reproduction straightforward.

Limitations and ethics are only partially treated. The paper discusses some failure modes in the appendix, but the main text is quite confident about safety and robustness despite adversarial accuracy remaining low after attack and despite the broader dual-use implications of controllable concept suppression.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: interpretable concept erasure in diffusion models without modifying the base model weights. The supervised SAE formulation is a clear and useful extension of prior unsupervised SAE-based unlearning, and the motivation around feature splitting is compelling.

Empirical results on UnlearnCanvas are strong within the SAE-based family: object unlearning improves substantially over SAeUron on UA/IRA/CRA, style results are competitive, and sequential object unlearning shows a meaningful advantage as more concepts are erased.

The paper includes several useful analyses beyond headline accuracy: score-distribution plots, k-NN evidence for single-latent informativeness, multiplier sensitivity, computational overhead, ablations over loss variants, and qualitative examples. These make the central mechanism more inspectable than in many concept-erasure papers.

The limitations and impact discussion are unusually candid. The authors acknowledge the closed-vocabulary constraint, within-group interference, scaling issues, and the uncertainty around newer diffusion architectures rather than hiding them.
weaknesses: The strongest conceptual claim, that SAEmnesia enforces one-to-one concept-latent mappings and eliminates feature splitting, is only partially supported. The evidence shows stronger top-latent concentration under the paper's score function and k-NN classification, but it does not rule out residual distributed information or demonstrate causal necessity/sufficiency of the single latent across diverse prompts and concepts.

The method depends on supervised labels derived from prompt templates and a fixed vocabulary of concepts. This makes the comparison to unsupervised SAE methods somewhat asymmetric: SAEmnesia gets explicit concept supervision, while the main baseline must discover concepts post hoc. The paper should more clearly separate gains due to supervision from gains due to the specific loss design.

The headline efficiency claim of a 96.67% reduction in hyperparameter search is somewhat overstated. The method still performs training-time grid search over loss hyperparameters, uses per-concept multiplier tuning in some settings, and the best NSFW result requires departing from the claimed single-latent setup. The reported search reduction is real for one narrow inference-time search procedure, but not the full practical cost of deploying the method.

The NSFW/nudity result is presented too strongly in the main text. The appendix shows that the default one-latent SAEmnesia setup is worse than SAeUron on I2P, and the best result requires steering two latents with an extremely large multiplier. This weakens the paper's central single-latent narrative and should be foregrounded rather than relegated to the appendix.

Evaluation is still concentrated on SD v1.x and UnlearnCanvas. The SDXL Turbo experiment is preliminary and has poor retain accuracy, omitted CRA, and an acknowledged evaluator domain mismatch. Thus the architecture-agnostic and scalability claims remain more aspirational than established.

Some experimental details needed for reproducibility are underspecified or scattered: exact prompt sets, checkpoint availability, activation extraction details across blocks/timesteps, multiplier selection protocol for all reported tables, and training duration are not fully clear from the main paper. Releasing code and trained SAE checkpoints would be important for others to build on the work.

The comparison to non-SAE methods is mixed: SalUn outperforms SAEmnesia on object unlearning average, and the paper's best overall table relies on combining object and style metrics. This is acceptable given the interpretability/reversibility goal, but the claims should be phrased more carefully as state-of-the-art among mechanistic/SAE approaches rather than broadly superior concept erasure.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: controllable concept erasure in diffusion models with an interpretable mechanism rather than full model fine-tuning.

The proposed supervised SAE idea is simple and potentially useful: adding concept-assignment and decorrelation losses can plausibly reduce feature splitting and make SAE-based interventions easier to target.

The main UnlearnCanvas object results show meaningful gains over the closest SAE-based baseline, SAeUron, especially in CRA and average score, and the paper includes additional experiments on sequential unlearning, adversarial prompts, style erasure, and nudity suppression.

The manuscript includes an honest limitations section covering closed-vocabulary behavior, within-group interference, scalability, and newer diffusion backbones, and it includes an impact statement acknowledging misuse and incomplete-unlearning risks.
weaknesses: The central claim of enforcing one-to-one concept-latent mappings is not fully established. The loss encourages assigned latents to activate for positive examples, but it does not clearly enforce injective concept-to-latent assignments or penalize activation of the same latent for absent or similar concepts. The authors themselves report within-group interference and cases such as cats/dogs overlap, weakening the strongest mechanistic claim.

The feature-centralization evidence is thin relative to the claim. The paper relies on a few score histograms, qualitative patch visualizations, and a k-NN comparison using top-scoring latents, but does not provide a rigorous aggregate metric over all concepts showing uniqueness, specificity, or stability of the learned mappings across seeds and prompts.

The empirical story is mixed. SAEmnesia is not best on object unlearning in Table 1 because SalUn has a higher object average, and the SDXL Turbo experiment is weak: average performance is only slightly above the no-unlearning baseline while IRA drops sharply. For I2P nudity removal, the single-latent version is worse than SAeUron and the reported best result requires a two-latent variant with an extreme multiplier, undercutting the single-latent narrative.

The efficiency claim is overstated. The 96.67% reduction counts only inference-time latent-combination search against SAeUron, while SAEmnesia adds substantial training overhead and itself requires supervised SAE training, grid search over loss weights, validation data, and per-concept multiplier tuning. The comparison does not present an end-to-end cost accounting.

The evaluation has reproducibility and fairness concerns. Important details such as full prompt lists, exact data construction, code/checkpoints, and adversarial prompt generation are not clearly provided. The Ring-A-Bell object adaptation uses Claude Sonnet 4.6 to generate prompt pairs, which is hard to reproduce and may introduce uncontrolled evaluation bias.

The adversarial robustness results are not sufficiently convincing. The white-box attack still causes a large UA drop, and the black-box adaptation appears custom rather than standard for object concepts. The explanation that stronger concept-neuron bonds cause robustness is speculative and not experimentally isolated.

Presentation is generally readable but repeatedly overclaims. Phrases such as eliminating feature splitting, enforcing one-to-one mappings, and establishing a step forward are stronger than the evidence supports, especially given the acknowledged interference, the need for multiple latents in nudity removal, and sensitivity to hyperparameters shown in the appendix.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: interpretable concept erasure in diffusion models. The core idea of adding supervised losses to SAE training to reduce feature splitting is simple, well-motivated, and useful.

The empirical results on UnlearnCanvas are strong for an SAE-based method. SAEmnesia improves over SAeUron on object unlearning across UA, IRA, CRA, and average score, and the appendix reports standard deviations over four seeds.

The paper provides several forms of evidence beyond a single benchmark table: score-distribution plots, k-NN evidence for feature centralization, qualitative visualizations, sequential unlearning, adversarial robustness, nudity suppression, and style-unlearning results.

The method has practical appeal because it preserves the base diffusion model and performs reversible inference-time steering. The reduction in latent-combination search relative to unsupervised SAE unlearning is a meaningful usability improvement.

The limitations and impact statement are reasonably candid. The authors acknowledge closed-vocabulary constraints, interference among similar concepts, scaling concerns for open vocabularies, and uncertainty on newer transformer-based diffusion models.
weaknesses: Some central claims are overstated. The manuscript repeatedly says it enforces or eliminates feature splitting via one-to-one concept-latent mappings, but the evidence is mostly benchmark- and score-based, not a rigorous demonstration that concepts are uniquely localized. Nudity unlearning also requires two latents, and the authors acknowledge within-group interference.

The strongest evaluation is concentrated on SD v1.5 and UnlearnCanvas, with only preliminary SDXL Turbo results. The SDXL result improves UA but has a large IRA drop, so architectural generality remains only partially supported.

The computational-efficiency claim is useful but somewhat narrow. The 96.67% reduction counts inference-time latent-combination search relative to SAeUron, but the proposed method introduces supervised training, a 27-configuration loss-hyperparameter grid, and per-concept multiplier choices. The comparison would be stronger with total wall-clock cost for a full unlearning workflow.

The adversarial robustness section is promising but not fully convincing. The custom Ring-A-Bell adaptation uses prompts generated by Claude and the threat model details are brief, making it hard to judge whether the comparison is standardized or reproducible.

Reproducibility is adequate but not excellent. The paper reports key SAE settings, loss hyperparameters, hardware, and some standard deviations, but does not clearly specify all training details such as number of epochs, dataset sizes after activation extraction, random seeds, exact prompt lists, or whether code/checkpoints for SAEmnesia will be released.

The presentation is generally clear, but the paper occasionally uses stronger language than the evidence warrants, and some appendix results reveal fragility: high beta can produce white images, similar concepts still interfere, and nudity suppression needs a very large multiplier in the Top-2 variant.
